subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
passage: In the coaching centre's small classroom, the teacher was solving a probability problem on the board. Pradeep watched the boy in front of him, Chaitanya, who had a frown and had stopped writing. Was he bored? Puzzled? Pradeep couldn't tell. Chaitanya's pen tapped slowly against his page, and once he glanced at the clock. Pradeep almost told the boy beside him that Chaitanya looked bored, but stopped himself. When the teacher let them work alone, Pradeep leaned forward and whispered, "Are you stuck on step three?" Chaitanya let out a breath. "Yes. I've been staring at it for ages and I'm not sure why the number changes." "Same here. Let's ask." They raised their hands together.

qa.q: Which problem was the teacher solving on the board?
qa.a: The teacher was solving a probability problem.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya have been thinking when he frowned and stopped writing?
qa.a: He was probably puzzled about a step he couldn't follow, though a frown and a glance at the clock could also have meant boredom.

qa.q: Why was whispering a question better than telling the other boy that Chaitanya looked bored?
qa.a: The cues were only hints, and asking gave Pradeep the truth; the guess would have been wrong.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have felt watching Chaitanya frown?
qa.a: Pradeep felt unsure whether Chaitanya was bored or puzzled, and held back from guessing aloud until he could ask directly.

grounding: A teen tries to tell whether a classmate is puzzled or bored, treats cues as hints and asks.

passage:
Hi Suraj,
I owe you an apology. During the group study on Thursday I saw you staring out of the window and giving one-word answers, and I told Manoj you were bored and didn't care about the project. I only had your face and your voice, and I filled in the rest myself. Then Kavya said you seemed lost, and I finally asked you outright. You said you hadn't understood the second section and felt awkward saying so. That was very different from what I'd guessed. I'm sorry for calling you bored behind your back. Can we go through the section on Saturday? I'll bring the notes.
Naveen

qa.q: What did Naveen see Suraj doing during the group study?
qa.a: Naveen saw Suraj staring out of the window and giving one-word answers.

qa.q: What was Suraj actually feeling during the study session?
qa.a: Suraj was confused about the second section and awkward about saying so, which was different from the boredom Naveen guessed.

qa.q: What could Naveen do differently next time Naveen isn't sure about someone's attention?
qa.a: Naveen could ask directly and kindly straight away, instead of guessing and telling others.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt on learning what Suraj was really feeling?
qa.a: Naveen felt sorry for guessing and saying it behind Suraj's back, and wanted to make up for it by going through the section together on Saturday.

grounding: A teen reads a classmate's face and voice as boredom, then learns by asking that it was confusion.

subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
passage:
Kishore, you asked how my tutoring thing went. So, I'm Aadhya, and every Saturday I help Class 6 kids with maths at the community centre.
First week, there was this boy, Ronak, who frowned the whole time. Arms crossed, eyes narrowed. I thought, great, he's bored. He hates me. So I talked faster to get it over with.
Next week, same frown. So I stopped and just asked, "Ronak, are you bored, or is something confusing?"
He looked shocked. "Confusing! The fractions part. I didn't want to say."
I'd read his frown completely wrong. It was concentration, and confusion. Not boredom at all.
Meanwhile the girl next to him, who smiled and nodded the whole time? She'd understood nothing either. Her smile was politeness.
So now I don't trust faces. I ask one question every ten minutes. "Still with me?"

qa.q: Where does Aadhya help Class 6 kids with maths?
qa.a: At the community centre.

qa.q: What was Aadhya thinking when Ronak frowned the first week?
qa.a: Aadhya felt discouraged and assumed Ronak was bored and disliked the tutoring, so rushed through the lesson.

qa.q: What did Aadhya change after learning the frown meant confusion?
qa.a: Aadhya now asks a quick "Still with me?" every ten minutes instead of trusting faces.

qa.q: How was Ronak feeling during those sessions?
qa.a: Ronak was confused by the fractions and too shy to say so, which his frown hid.

grounding: The spoken account shows a teenager misreading a frown as boredom and a smile as understanding, and learning to ask instead of assuming.

subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
passage:
I'm Mohit, and I watched Sunaina present her coding project to our class on Friday. She was explaining loops, really fast, clicking through slides.
She kept looking at the back row. Three boys were leaning back, chins on hands, eyes half closed. I saw her face drop. She sped up even more. I guessed she thought they were bored.
But I sat near them. One was actually copying her code into his notebook. Another was frowning at the screen like he was trying to follow. I couldn't tell about the third. Maybe bored, maybe tired.
At the end, Sunaina said, a bit flatly, "Any questions? Probably not."
The frowning boy put his hand up. "Can you go back to the second loop? I didn't get where it stops."
Sunaina looked surprised. Then she smiled and went back. Three more hands went up after that.

qa.q: What was one boy in the back row copying?
qa.a: He was copying her code into his notebook.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when she looked at the back row?
qa.a: Sunaina felt discouraged and anxious, her face dropping, because she read their leaning back as boredom.

qa.q: What could Sunaina try next time?
qa.a: Pause and ask a question partway through, since faces and posture are only hints, not proof of boredom.

qa.q: How did the frowning boy actually feel about the presentation?
qa.a: He was interested but confused, trying to follow where the second loop stopped.

grounding: A classmate's account shows a teenager misreading faces as boredom, while they actually showed interest and confusion.

subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
passage:
Monday: Sachin started tutoring Ujjwal for the physics retest. Ujjwal yawned twice and stared out of the window. Sachin thought, he doesn't care. He finished early and went home annoyed.
Wednesday: Ujjwal yawned again, rubbing his eyes. But this time Sachin noticed he was also chewing his pen and his eyebrows were pinched together. Sachin stopped. "Are you bored, or confused, or tired?"
Ujjwal let out a breath. "All three? I'm helping my uncle at the shop till eleven every night. And I honestly don't get what acceleration even is."
Friday: Sachin switched to examples. A cricket ball, a scooter speeding up at a signal. They met right after school, not in the evening. Ujjwal leaned forward the whole hour.
"Oh!" he said at the end. "It's just how fast the speed changes."
Sachin grinned. He'd almost given up on Monday.

qa.q: Until what time does Ujjwal help his uncle at the shop?
qa.a: Till eleven every night.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal actually feeling during the lessons?
qa.a: Ujjwal was tired from late nights and confused about acceleration, not simply bored.

qa.q: What helped Sachin read the situation correctly?
qa.a: Noticing mixed cues on Wednesday and asking directly whether Ujjwal was bored, confused or tired, instead of assuming.

qa.q: What would change if Sachin had kept assuming boredom?
qa.a: Ujjwal might have felt judged as lazy and been even more lost before the retest.

grounding: The three beats show a teenager misreading yawns as boredom, then asking and discovering tiredness and confusion.

subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
passage: Pema, you say your study group looks bored when you explain? Let me tell you about your Jeevan Tata at fifteen. I was in charge of our group's model of the heart, and I was very proud of my explanations. There was a boy called Nanda who sat through them rubbing his eyes, chin on his fist. I decided he was bored, maybe even mocking me, so I started talking faster and louder at him. Sister Agnes, our science teacher, watched this for a day. Then she said, "Jeevan, you have not asked him one thing." So I asked him, a bit rudely, "Are you even following?" Nanda went red and said, "No. I got lost at the valves on Monday and was too ashamed to say." The fist under the chin was him trying to keep up. After that I stopped every few minutes and asked, "Where are you?" Your face tells me you are interested now. But I will ask anyway: are you?

qa.q: What was Jeevan in charge of in the group?
qa.a: Jeevan was in charge of the group's model of the heart.

qa.q: What was young Jeevan feeling when he decided Nanda was bored?
qa.a: Jeevan felt proud of the explanations and then irritated, even slighted, thinking he was being mocked, which made him talk faster and louder.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed things?
qa.a: Asking Nanda directly, after Sister Agnes pointed it out, revealed confusion, and stopping every few minutes to ask 'Where are you?' kept the group with him.

qa.q: What was it like for Nanda during those explanations?
qa.a: Nanda had been lost since Monday and was ashamed to say so, rubbing his eyes and propping his chin while trying to keep up.

grounding: It shows a teenager misreading a classmate's face as boredom when it was confusion, told as an elder's memory in which asking beats assuming.
